paper.title: Universal Daycare and Mothers' Working Lifetime
paper.code_data_availability: Supplementary data: 'The authors were granted an exemption to publish their data because access to the data is restricted. …

registers.role: sample frame; neighbourhood (parish) and municipality of residence on 4 November 1970; pre-1980 educational attainment
variables_mentioned: educational attainment and date of achievement

registers.name_in_paper: Supplementary Pension Fund Register (in Danish: ATP)
registers.role: outcomes: labour market participation before 1980, full-time employment, average weekly hours of work

registers.name_in_paper: earnings registered annually by the tax authorities
registers.role: outcomes: log earnings; participation from 1980 (any positive earnings)
controls (mother's educational attainment before the first birth); outcome (additional education after the first birth)

registers.name_in_paper: daycare yearbooks (National Board of Social Services, 1968-72; Tvenstrup, 1975) and, from 1976, the administrative registers
registers.role: treatment: year of the first daycare opening in each neighbourhood

registers.name_in_paper: complete fertility histories in the Danish administrative data (personal identifiers linking parents and children)
registers.role: outcomes: number of children, spacing, half-siblings

registers.name_in_paper: cohabitation / address information for mothers and fathers
registers.role: outcomes: parental separation and new partner in the year the first child turns 16

registers.name_in_paper: a census on the number of employed women for each neighbourhood in the year 1960
registers.role: aggregate validation data for the neighbourhood-level event study

registers.name_in_paper: data from the Danish Geodata Agency
registers.role: linkage: parish latitude and longitude for the map and for the distance measure

linkages: The Danish registers contain a unique identifier for each individual and a link between children and parents, making it possible to combine data from several registers and families
mothers are assigned daycare access by matching the neighbourhood of daycare in the years after the birth of the first child to the mother's neighbourhood (parish) of residence in the 1970 census
individual ATP data aggregated to neighbourhood-year counts of employed women for 1964-2003, combined with the 1960 census counts and the daycare opening panel for 1940-1993
mother's parish of birth linked to her 1970 parish of residence via latitude and longitude to compute distance moved

sample.universe: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975
sample.unit_of_observation: mother (mother-year in the contemporaneous and long-run outcome panels; neighbourhood-year in the event study of Equation 3)
selection_rules: start from all women in the 1970 census data (all women resident in Denmark in 1970)
keep those who had their first child between 1964 and 1975
drop mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent)
drop mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent)
for the spacing analysis, keep mothers with more than one child (305,504)
for the separation and new-partner outcomes, keep mothers with observed addresses in the year the first child turns 16 (365,954)
for the migration check, keep mothers with a non-missing birth parish (328,330; birth place is missing for 11.4 percent) and, in Panel B, exclude mothers born or residing on Bornholm (324,433)
for the event study of Equation (4), keep mothers in the 697 parishes that implemented their first daycare between 1954 and 1990 (119,885 mothers)
sample.period: first births 1964-1975; outcomes followed four through 34 years after the first birth; earnings 1980-2015; neighbourhood aggregates 1960-2003

construction_notes: earnings are adjusted to 2016 US-prices and converted to log points; the measure excludes unemployment insurance and other social benefits, so log earnings are undefined without a job and the earnings estimates are conditional on employment

participation is coded from any ATP contribution within the year before 1980 and from any positive earnings from 1980; the paper states results are not sensitive to the different definitions of participation
full-time employment is a full ATP contribution, corresponding to a minimum of 30 hours of work a week throughout the year

average weekly hours of work are constructed from the annual ATP contribution bands (one-third for 10-19 hours, two-thirds for 20-29 hours, full for 30+ hours a week), so a one-third contribution can mean 10 hours a week all year or full-time for a third of the year
the wage rate is not used as an outcome because work hours are not observed below 10 and above 30 hours a week

mother's educational attainment is defined before the first birth; for the 50 percent whose first child was born before 1970 the education is assumed pre-birth if its length plus the normal starting age is less than her age at the first birth, otherwise set to the mandatory level (0.02 percent); two equally sized groups are defined (no post-secondary vs. some post-secondary schooling)

two summary daycare measures are used in the fertility, spacing and separation analyses: an indicator for daycare availability for children up to age two and an indicator for children aged three to six, both measured in the year of the first birth, plus their interaction; among mothers with daycare for ages three to six, 53 percent also had daycare for ages up to two
placebo daycare openings for neighbourhoods without a daycare are drawn from a normal distribution with mean 1970 and standard deviation 11, mimicking the observed roll-out

the neighbourhood-level event-study regressions are weighted by population size and the estimated level effects are converted into percentages by scaling with the average number of employed women at the corresponding event time

effect sizes in Figures 5, 6 and 7 are plotted in percent, each point estimate divided by the mean of the dependent variable in the corresponding year (means in Appendix Table A.3, which is not part of the article PDF)
distance moved is measured in 100 km between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence using parish latitude and longitude
standard errors are clustered at the parish (neighbourhood) level throughout

claims.statement: Daycare availability in the parish in the year the first born child turns four is unrelated to mothers' labour force participation measured 6 years before the birth of the first child.

treatment.label: Daycare year 4 (daycare availability in the year the first born child turns four)

register_source.value: daycare yearbooks (National Board of Social Services, 1968-72; Tvenstrup, 1975) for 1964-1975 and the administrative registers from 1976, matched to the mother's parish of residence on 4 November 1970 in the 1970 census

definition.value: Indicator for daycare availability in the mother's parish (1970 census parish of residence) in the year her first born child turns four; used as the explanatory variable in all long-run regressions

timing.value: the calendar year in which the mother's first born child turns four

register_source.value: Supplementary Pension Fund Register (ATP) before 1980; annual earnings from the tax registers from 1980

definition.value: Dummy for labour market participation: prior to 1980 one if any ATP contributions were made within the year; after 1980 one if the mother had any positive earnings within the year

timing.value: 6 years before the birth of the first child

units.value: proportion of mothers (a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point)

estimand.target_population: Main-sample mothers observed in the labour market registers in the given year before the birth of their first child (173,342 mothers six years before the first birth, rising to 303,174 two years before)
estimand.time_horizon: outcome measured 6 years before the birth of the first child

population.description: Main-sample mothers observed in the labour market registers in the given year before the birth of their first child (173,342 mothers six years before the first birth, rising to 303,174 two years before)
population.ages: mean age at first birth 23.7 years
population.period: first births 1964-1975; outcomes followed up to 34 years after the first birth
population.selection: women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975; mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent) and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent) are dropped; further conditioned on being observed in the ATP data in the given pre-birth year

identification.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the daycare roll-out the labour market outcomes of mothers residing in neighbourhoods that implemented daycare at different times would have evolved along parallel trends
key_assumptions.supported_by: an event study on neighbourhood-level aggregated counts of employed women 1960-2003, comparing neighbourhoods that open a daycare with neighbourhoods assigned a placebo opening (Figure 3); estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed before the first birth (Table 2); and an event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)

key_assumptions.assumption: Homogeneous average treatment effects between the treated neighbourhoods and over time, which together with parallel trends makes alpha the average treatment effect on the treated
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper acknowledges the two-way fixed effects literature and reports that the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator gives similar results for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)

key_assumptions.assumption: No selective migration: parents do not select into a neighbourhood on the basis of daycare availability, so the match between the mother's 1970 census parish of residence and parish daycare availability is not endogenous
key_assumptions.supported_by: regressions of the distance between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence on daycare availability (Table 9): the raw association disappears once parish fixed effects are included, and the result is robust to excluding Bornholm

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the parish
implies_edges.to: mother's parish of residence in the 1970 census

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across parishes: mothers do not obtain childcare in parishes other than the one they live in, so parish-level daycare availability captures the mother's own access
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the author states she cannot rule out some contamination bias and argues it would bias the estimates downward

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in neighbouring parishes
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market and family outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: Individual daycare enrolment is not observed, so alpha is an intention-to-treat effect of local availability rather than an effect of enrolment
key_assumptions.supported_by: the author notes that enrolment would most likely be endogenous and therefore reports reduced-form availability effects

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: labour market outcomes of women before the birth of their first child are not affected by the daycare that is available in their parish in the year that child later turns four
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 regressions of pre-birth participation, full-time employment and hours on daycare access in the year the first child turns four; insignificant six, five and four years before the first birth but positive and significant for hours three years before and for participation and hours two years before

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the year the first child turns four
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market outcomes before the first birth

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on surviving in Denmark until the first child turns 16 and on being observed in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper reports the share dropped (2.2 percent immigrant background, 0.6 percent emigration or death) but offers no test of the conditioning

implies_edges.from: mother remains resident and alive until the first child turns 16
implies_edges.to: sample inclusion

threats_discussed: selective migration of parents into neighbourhoods with daycare availability
assignment of daycare status on the mother's 1970 address, which is not predetermined for mothers whose first child was born before 1970
daycare centres opening in or around the largest cities and their suburbs, where job opportunities were better
contamination bias from mothers using childcare in parishes other than their own
inconsistency of the register birth-registration variable, which has a data break in 1978
bias of two-way fixed effects estimators under treatment effect heterogeneity across groups or time
robustness_checks: estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed six through two years before the first birth (Table 2)
neighbourhood-level event study of employed women around actual and placebo daycare openings (Figure 3)
the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)
event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)
regressions of distance moved on daycare availability, with and without Bornholm (Table 9)
alternative daycare assignment based on the first born child's parish of birth, excluding pre-1978 births in parishes with a hospital and extending the sample to children born until 1990 (Figure 7)
excluding the three largest municipalities (Appendix Figure A.4)
excluding the suburbs of the two largest cities (Appendix Figure A.5)
alternative definitions of labour market participation
unresolved_confounders: contamination bias: mothers may find childcare options in parishes other than the one they live in, which the author cannot rule out but argues biases the estimates downward
for mothers who had their first child before 1970 (50 percent of the sample) the 1970 address used to assign daycare status was not predetermined

claims.statement: Daycare availability in the mother's parish 5 years after the birth of the first child raises mothers' labour force participation in that same year.

treatment.label: DC_nt (daycare availability in neighbourhood n at time t)

register_source.value: daycare yearbooks (National Board of Social Services, 1968-72; Tvenstrup, 1975) for 1964-1975 and the administrative registers from 1976, matched to the mother's parish of residence on 4 November 1970 in the 1970 census

definition.value: Indicator taking the value one if neighbourhood (parish) n has implemented daycare for the relevant age group of the child at time t and zero otherwise; the mother's neighbourhood is her parish of residence in the 1970 census

timing.value: 5 years after the birth of the first child

register_source.value: Supplementary Pension Fund Register (ATP) before 1980; annual earnings from the tax registers from 1980

definition.value: Dummy for labour market participation: prior to 1980 one if any ATP contributions were made within the year; after 1980 one if the mother had any positive earnings within the year

timing.value: 5 years after the birth of the first child

units.value: proportion of mothers (a coefficient of 0.01 is one percentage point)

magnitude.interpretation: 7.0 (0.035/0.50) percent more likely to participate in the labour market in the year their first born child turns five

estimand.target_population: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: outcome and daycare availability both measured 5 years after the birth of the first child

population.description: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers

estimand.target_population: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers

population.description: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers

population.selection: women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975; mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent) and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent) are dropped

identification.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the daycare roll-out the labour market outcomes of mothers residing in neighbourhoods that implemented daycare at different times would have evolved along parallel trends
key_assumptions.supported_by: an event study on neighbourhood-level aggregated counts of employed women 1960-2003, comparing neighbourhoods that open a daycare with neighbourhoods assigned a placebo opening (Figure 3); estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed before the first birth (Table 2); and an event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)

key_assumptions.assumption: Homogeneous average treatment effects between the treated neighbourhoods and over time, which together with parallel trends makes alpha the average treatment effect on the treated
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper acknowledges the two-way fixed effects literature and reports that the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator gives similar results for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)

key_assumptions.assumption: No selective migration: parents do not select into a neighbourhood on the basis of daycare availability, so the match between the mother's 1970 census parish of residence and parish daycare availability is not endogenous
key_assumptions.supported_by: regressions of the distance between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence on daycare availability (Table 9): the raw association disappears once parish fixed effects are included, and the result is robust to excluding Bornholm

estimand.target_population: Main-sample mothers with distance information, excluding mothers born or residing on the island Bornholm, a geographical outlier; 324,433 mothers

population.description: Main-sample mothers with distance information, excluding mothers born or residing on the island Bornholm, a geographical outlier; 324,433 mothers
population.ages: mean age at first birth 23.7 years
population.period: first births 1964-1975; outcomes followed up to 34 years after the first birth
population.selection: women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975; mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent) and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent) are dropped; further restricted to mothers with a non-missing birth parish and excluding Bornholm

identification.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the daycare roll-out the labour market outcomes of mothers residing in neighbourhoods that implemented daycare at different times would have evolved along parallel trends
key_assumptions.supported_by: an event study on neighbourhood-level aggregated counts of employed women 1960-2003, comparing neighbourhoods that open a daycare with neighbourhoods assigned a placebo opening (Figure 3); estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed before the first birth (Table 2); and an event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)

key_assumptions.assumption: Homogeneous average treatment effects between the treated neighbourhoods and over time, which together with parallel trends makes alpha the average treatment effect on the treated
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper acknowledges the two-way fixed effects literature and reports that the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator gives similar results for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)

key_assumptions.assumption: No selective migration: parents do not select into a neighbourhood on the basis of daycare availability, so the match between the mother's 1970 census parish of residence and parish daycare availability is not endogenous
key_assumptions.supported_by: regressions of the distance between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence on daycare availability (Table 9): the raw association disappears once parish fixed effects are included, and the result is robust to excluding Bornholm

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the parish
implies_edges.to: mother's parish of residence in the 1970 census

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across parishes: mothers do not obtain childcare in parishes other than the one they live in, so parish-level daycare availability captures the mother's own access
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the author states she cannot rule out some contamination bias and argues it would bias the estimates downward

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in neighbouring parishes
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market and family outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: Individual daycare enrolment is not observed, so alpha is an intention-to-treat effect of local availability rather than an effect of enrolment

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: labour market outcomes of women before the birth of their first child are not affected by the daycare that is available in their parish in the year that child later turns four

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the year the first child turns four
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market outcomes before the first birth

key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper reports the share dropped (2.2 percent immigrant background, 0.6 percent emigration or death) but offers no test of the conditioning

outcomes_examined_not_reported: the wage rate, which the paper says it does not include as an outcome because work hours are not observed for those working less than 10 and above 30 hours a week

claims.statement: Daycare availability in the year the first born child turns four raises mothers' labour force participation 10 years after the birth of the first child by 5.5 percent of the mean participation rate in that year.

treatment.label: Daycare year 4 (daycare availability in the year the first born child turns four)

register_source.value: daycare yearbooks (National Board of Social Services, 1968-72; Tvenstrup, 1975) for 1964-1975 and the administrative registers from 1976, matched to the mother's parish of residence on 4 November 1970 in the 1970 census

definition.value: Indicator for daycare availability in the mother's parish (1970 census parish of residence) in the year her first born child turns four; used as the explanatory variable in all long-run regressions

timing.value: the calendar year in which the mother's first born child turns four

register_source.value: Supplementary Pension Fund Register (ATP) before 1980; annual earnings from the tax registers from 1980

definition.value: Dummy for labour market participation: prior to 1980 one if any ATP contributions were made within the year; after 1980 one if the mother had any positive earnings within the year

timing.value: 10 years after the birth of the first child (when the first child is 10)

units.value: percent of the mean of the dependent variable in the corresponding year

estimand.target_population: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers
estimand.time_horizon: 10 years after the birth of the first child

population.description: All women in the 1970 Danish census (i.e., all women resident in Denmark in 1970) who had their first child between 1964 and 1975, after dropping mothers with an immigrant background and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before the first child turns 16; 370,602 mothers
population.ages: mean age at first birth 23.7 years
population.period: first births 1964-1975; outcomes followed up to 34 years after the first birth
population.selection: women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975; mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent) and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent) are dropped

identification.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the daycare roll-out the labour market outcomes of mothers residing in neighbourhoods that implemented daycare at different times would have evolved along parallel trends
key_assumptions.supported_by: an event study on neighbourhood-level aggregated counts of employed women 1960-2003, comparing neighbourhoods that open a daycare with neighbourhoods assigned a placebo opening (Figure 3); estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed before the first birth (Table 2); and an event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)

key_assumptions.assumption: Homogeneous average treatment effects between the treated neighbourhoods and over time, which together with parallel trends makes alpha the average treatment effect on the treated
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper acknowledges the two-way fixed effects literature and reports that the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator gives similar results for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)

key_assumptions.assumption: No selective migration: parents do not select into a neighbourhood on the basis of daycare availability, so the match between the mother's 1970 census parish of residence and parish daycare availability is not endogenous
key_assumptions.supported_by: regressions of the distance between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence on daycare availability (Table 9): the raw association disappears once parish fixed effects are included, and the result is robust to excluding Bornholm

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the parish
implies_edges.to: mother's parish of residence in the 1970 census

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across parishes: mothers do not obtain childcare in parishes other than the one they live in, so parish-level daycare availability captures the mother's own access
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the author states she cannot rule out some contamination bias and argues it would bias the estimates downward

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in neighbouring parishes
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market and family outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: Individual daycare enrolment is not observed, so alpha is an intention-to-treat effect of local availability rather than an effect of enrolment
key_assumptions.supported_by: the author notes that enrolment would most likely be endogenous and therefore reports reduced-form availability effects

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: labour market outcomes of women before the birth of their first child are not affected by the daycare that is available in their parish in the year that child later turns four
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 regressions of pre-birth participation, full-time employment and hours on daycare access in the year the first child turns four; insignificant six, five and four years before the first birth but positive and significant for hours three years before and for participation and hours two years before

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the year the first child turns four
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market outcomes before the first birth

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection on surviving in Denmark until the first child turns 16 and on being observed in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper reports the share dropped (2.2 percent immigrant background, 0.6 percent emigration or death) but offers no test of the conditioning

implies_edges.from: mother remains resident and alive until the first child turns 16
implies_edges.to: sample inclusion

threats_discussed: selective migration of parents into neighbourhoods with daycare availability
assignment of daycare status on the mother's 1970 address, which is not predetermined for mothers whose first child was born before 1970
daycare centres opening in or around the largest cities and their suburbs, where job opportunities were better
contamination bias from mothers using childcare in parishes other than their own
inconsistency of the register birth-registration variable, which has a data break in 1978
bias of two-way fixed effects estimators under treatment effect heterogeneity across groups or time
robustness_checks: estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed six through two years before the first birth (Table 2)
neighbourhood-level event study of employed women around actual and placebo daycare openings (Figure 3)
the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)
event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)
regressions of distance moved on daycare availability, with and without Bornholm (Table 9)
alternative daycare assignment based on the first born child's parish of birth, excluding pre-1978 births in parishes with a hospital and extending the sample to children born until 1990 (Figure 7)
excluding the three largest municipalities (Appendix Figure A.4)
excluding the suburbs of the two largest cities (Appendix Figure A.5)
alternative definitions of labour market participation
unresolved_confounders: contamination bias: mothers may find childcare options in parishes other than the one they live in, which the author cannot rule out but argues biases the estimates downward
for mothers who had their first child before 1970 (50 percent of the sample) the 1970 address used to assign daycare status was not predetermined

estimation.specification: Equation (2) estimated by OLS separately at each horizon, with year and parish fixed effects and a full set of dummies for the mother's year of birth; point estimates divided by the mean of the dependent variable in the corresponding year
controls: full set of dummies for mother's year of birth
estimation.clustering: standard errors clustered at the parish (neighbourhood) level

source_table.value: Figure 5, panel (a) Participation rate, 10 years after the first childbirth

parental separation from the father of the first born child

evidence.annotation: Note- The figure shows the effects of daycare in the year the first born child turns four on (a) the participation rate four through 34 years after the first childbirth relative to the sample mean, (b) full-time employment four through 34 years after the first childbirth relative to the sample mean, (c) log earnings (conditional on employment) 16 through 34 years after the first childbirth, and (d) hours of work per week four through 34 years after the first childbirth relative to the sample mean. claims.statement: For mothers with some post-secondary schooling, daycare availability in the year the first born child turns four has no statistically significant effect on labour market earnings.

treatment.label: Daycare year 4 (daycare availability in the year the first born child turns four)

register_source.value: daycare yearbooks (National Board of Social Services, 1968-72; Tvenstrup, 1975) for 1964-1975 and the administrative registers from 1976, matched to the mother's parish of residence on 4 November 1970 in the 1970 census

definition.value: Indicator for daycare availability in the mother's parish (1970 census parish of residence) in the year her first born child turns four; used as the explanatory variable in all long-run regressions

timing.value: the calendar year in which the mother's first born child turns four

register_source.value: annual earnings registered by the tax authorities (Statistics Denmark registers, 1980-2015)

definition.value: Annual labour market earnings registered by the tax authorities, adjusted to 2016 US-prices and converted to log points; the measure excludes unemployment insurance and other social benefits, so log earnings are undefined without a job and the estimates are conditional on employment

timing.value: 16 through 34 years after the birth of the first child

units.value: percent (log points scaled by the mean of the dependent variable)

estimand.target_population: Main-sample mothers with some post-secondary schooling (vocational training, college, or university) obtained before the first birth; 184,475 mothers
estimand.time_horizon: 16 through 34 years after the birth of the first child

population.description: Main-sample mothers with some post-secondary schooling (vocational training, college, or university) obtained before the first birth; 184,475 mothers
population.ages: mean age at first birth 23.7 years
population.period: first births 1964-1975; outcomes followed up to 34 years after the first birth
population.selection: women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census with a first birth in 1964-1975; mothers with an immigrant background (2.2 percent) and mothers who move out of Denmark or pass away before their first child turns 16 (0.6 percent) are dropped

identification.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: in the absence of the daycare roll-out the labour market outcomes of mothers residing in neighbourhoods that implemented daycare at different times would have evolved along parallel trends
key_assumptions.supported_by: an event study on neighbourhood-level aggregated counts of employed women 1960-2003, comparing neighbourhoods that open a daycare with neighbourhoods assigned a placebo opening (Figure 3); estimates of daycare access on labour market outcomes observed before the first birth (Table 2); and an event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)

key_assumptions.assumption: Homogeneous average treatment effects between the treated neighbourhoods and over time, which together with parallel trends makes alpha the average treatment effect on the treated
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper acknowledges the two-way fixed effects literature and reports that the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator gives similar results for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)

key_assumptions.assumption: No selective migration: parents do not select into a neighbourhood on the basis of daycare availability, so the match between the mother's 1970 census parish of residence and parish daycare availability is not endogenous
key_assumptions.supported_by: regressions of the distance between the mother's parish of birth and her 1970 parish of residence on daycare availability (Table 9): the raw association disappears once parish fixed effects are included, and the result is robust to excluding Bornholm

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in the parish
implies_edges.to: mother's parish of residence in the 1970 census

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across parishes: mothers do not obtain childcare in parishes other than the one they live in, so parish-level daycare availability captures the mother's own access
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the author states she cannot rule out some contamination bias and argues it would bias the estimates downward

implies_edges.from: daycare availability in neighbouring parishes
implies_edges.to: mother's labour market and family outcomes

key_assumptions.assumption: Individual daycare enrolment is not observed, so alpha is an intention-to-treat effect of local availability rather than an effect of enrolment
key_assumptions.supported_by: the author notes that enrolment would most likely be endogenous and therefore reports reduced-form availability effects

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: labour market outcomes of women before the birth of their first child are not affected by the daycare that is available in their parish in the year that child later turns four
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 2 regressions of pre-birth participation, full-time employment and hours on daycare access in the year the first child turns four; insignificant six, five and four years before the first birth but positive and significant for hours three years before and for participation and hours two years before

the Borusyak et al. (2024) imputation estimator for the neighbourhood-level event study (Appendix Figure A.3)
event study by the age of the first born child at the first daycare opening (Figure 4)
regressions of distance moved on daycare availability, with and without Bornholm (Table 9)

alternative definitions of labour market participation
